## Glossary

**ACS:** American Community Survey

**BWN/A:** Boil Water Notices / Advisories

**CEJST:** Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool

**CONUS:** Contiguous United States

**CVI:** Climate Vulnerability Index

**CWA:** Clean Water Act

**CWS:** Community Water System

**DWSRF:** Drinking Water State Revolving Fund

**EPA:** Environmental Protection Agency

**FIPS:** Federal Information Processing Standards

**FOIA:** Freedom of Information Act

**HUC:** Hydrologic Unit Code

**NHGIS:** National Historical Geographic Information System

**NPDES:** National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System

**PWSID:** Public Water System ID

**RMP:** Risk Management Plan

**SAB:** Service Area Boundary

**SDWA:** Safe Drinking Water Act

**SDWIS:** Safe Drinking Water Information System

**SVI:** Social Vulnerability Index

**UST:** Underground Storage Tank

**WBD:** Watershed Boundary Dataset

## Community Water System Service Area Boundaries {#raw_epa_sabs}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_epa_sabs -->

**Description:** This dataset contains the service area boundaries for Community Water Systems for the U.S. and select territories (Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands), which describes the geographic area that receives drinking water from a water system. Since the latest update in October 2025, over half of the ~50,000 water system service area boundaries are derived from authoritative data sources.

**Caveats:** Boundaries for water systems may be modeled, and/or overlap with other water systems. Please note there is one duplicated system in the raw dataset "ND2801430" (removed for the application) and a water system may be associated with more than one water system ID, "PR0005086; PR0005066" for example. This vintage is used for filtering all other datasets in the tool. Some states (North & South Dakota, for example) have service area boundaries that cover most of the state; based on the metadata from the EPA, this appears to reflect how the state reported their data.

**EPIC's data score:** 83%. This score is based on the data contained within the service area boundary dataset (water system ID, water system name, etc.) and the geometries of these boundaries. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 11 different variables. Combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe, this produced the mean quality score above. For boundaries, EPIC checked for the presence of overlaps, which produced a quality score of 82% (approximately 82% of service areas do not overlap with other service area boundaries). This produced a mean score for the dataset.

**Recommended uses:** Estimating the area served by a community water system. Estimating the population characteristics of a community served by a water system.

**Methods:** EPA SABs were downloaded from GitHub. When a PWSID contained multiple boundaries (specifically: "FL1070685", "FL1190789", "FL6580531", "IA2573701", "MT0001923", "VA5019052"), the boundaries were merged into a single multipolygon. One distinct SAB appeared to be duplicated, "ND2801430"; the boundary generated by the EPA ORD was retained, as the original source appeared to just contain water districts. A couple of boundaries have multiple water system IDs (e.g. "PR0005086; PR0005066") and were kept as a single record - meaning water system information may be missing for this record (since it contains two separate water systems), but interpolated data (income, climate vulnerability indexes, etc.) is present for this boundary. Invalid geometries were corrected using `st_make_valid()`, and boundaries were simplified using `st_simplify()`. All area calculations used `st_area()` with an Albers equal area projection (crs = 5070).

## Safe Drinking Water Information System {#raw_sdwa}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_sdwa -->

**Description:** Water system violation, enforcement, and system information from the federal Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS).

**Caveats:** There are known issues with water systems underreporting their violations. The source water protection code is only available for certain states in SDWIS, because SDWIS tracks whether the system has implemented source water protection according to state policy. The maximum age of a system is often set at ~45 years old because the "first_reported_date" in SDWIS is "1979-03-01" or early 1980; considering SDWA started in 1974, these systems may have been operating for longer, but this is likely the date they started being tracked by the EPA.

**EPIC's data score:** 76.6%. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 40 different variables. Combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe, this produced a mean quality score.

**Recommended uses:** Calculating the number and types of violations and enforcement actions a water system has had over the past years. Gathering water system characteristics (water system ID, name, years in operation, etc.).

**Methods:** Data were downloaded from the bulk SDWA download; the violations_enforcement dataset, the ref_code values, and the pub_water_systems dataset were pulled out. Since the violations and enforcement data contain duplicated rows and IDs by violation and enforcement action, a unique ID was created by concatenating the PWSID and violation ID, and duplicates were removed. Data were filtered based on water system IDs within the SABs dataset.

Disaggregated health-based violations by rule codes were selected where "is_health_based_ind" was "Y", filtered to "compl_per_begin_date" (the begin period in which the violation was identified), and merged using the ref_code dataset to identify specific rule violations. Violations were analyzed over the past 10 and 5 years (i.e., where the violation year is greater than the year the pipeline last ran minus 10 or 5 years). If the system has been operating for less than 5 or 10 years, relevant violation summaries were replaced with "Not Enough Data" to avoid incorrect comparisons across systems (this shows up as "NA" in the tool).

Open health-based violations are instances where "is_health_based_ind" is "Y" and the violation status was "addressed" or "unaddressed" (i.e., not "resolved" or "archived"). Violations over the past 5 or 10 years that required a public notification (simplified to "pn") were instances where public_notification_tier == 1 - all of these were health-based violations. Phone numbers, boolean values, and gw_sw_codes were standardized for the application.

## Drinking Water State Revolving Funds Awards {#raw_dwsrf}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_dwsrf -->

**Description:** This dataset contains downloaded data from EPA's State Revolving Fund Public Portal for federal fiscal years 2021-2025.

**Caveats:** This dataset only contains water systems that received Drinking Water State Revolving Funding from 2021-2025, or amendments during this time period. Principal forgiveness represents "Additional Subsidy Amount", which includes direct principal forgiveness as well as negative interest rates and grants. There are some peculiarities with latest assistance agreement dates, affecting two projects with dates of 1919 and 1997, likely due to data entry - these records are not removed for the purposes of the application.

**EPIC's data score:** 100%. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across the different variables. Combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe, this produced a mean quality score.

**Recommended uses:** Identifying which systems have or have not received assistance from the DWSRF program from 2021-2025.

**Methods:** Data was manually downloaded from the EPA's State Revolving Fund Public Portal. Three variables are created: data is grouped by PWSID to represent the total number of projects, total assistance corresponds to the Current Agreement Amount, and principal forgiveness represents "Additional Subsidy Amount" (which includes direct principal forgiveness as well as negative interest rates and grants).

## Census Variables {#clean_epa_sabs_crosswalk}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: clean_epa_sabs_crosswalk -->

**Description:** ACS 2021 estimates for EPA's Service Area Boundaries using methods developed by EPIC. This includes over 70 different census variables.

**Caveats:** The EPA ORD crosswalk is missing approximately 1,296 water systems. As a result, EPIC may be missing certain count variables for water systems but has estimated income variables (which were interpolated based on water system boundary).

**EPIC's data score:** 76%. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 30 different variables that were created after cleaning the crosswalked/interpolated dataset. Combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe, this produced a mean quality score of 76%.

**Recommended uses:** Estimation of the number of people captured within a service area and their main characteristics (race, ethnicity, income, etc.). Identifying water systems that may serve vulnerable communities (elderly, children, low income, etc.).

**Methods:** The census tract and service area boundary crosswalk file was downloaded from the EPA ORD GitHub website. This table uses Microsoft building footprints to weight census data to water system service area boundaries. Data from duplicated systems were removed (specifically: "FL1070685", "FL1190789", "FL6580531", "IA2573701", "MT0001923", "VA5019052"), as they sometimes produced weights greater than one. Data from the ACS 2021 5-year estimate were collected. All non-income variables were multiplied by the specific water system and tract weight, grouped by the water system ID, and summed to estimate totals at the water system level.

Prior to weighted interpolation, income variables (median household income, lowest quintile of income) were related to the percentage of the total universe (median household income divided by the sum of median household incomes across the entire U.S.) to generate a percentage that could be treated as spatially intensive. Weights for weighted interpolation were created using the number of households in census blocks from the 2020 decennial census. All spatial datasets used for weighting were projected to an Albers equal area projection (crs = 5070) prior to interpolating.

After interpolation, the percentage was multiplied by the total universe (i.e., sum of median household income across the entire U.S.) to relate the variable back to income. Water systems that overlap with multiple states were handled using a mean. Because census count variables and income variables are handled differently (a crosswalk file versus household weighted interpolation), there may be instances where a water system does not have census count estimates (e.g. total population) but has income estimates (e.g. median household income), and vice versa.

## Percent Change in Census Variables {#clean_epa_sabs_crosswalk_pct_change}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: clean_epa_sabs_crosswalk_pct_change -->

**Description:** The 10-year percent change in census variables for EPA's Service Area Boundaries using methods developed by EPIC. This includes over 70 different census variables.

**Caveats:** Not all census variables were available for the 2011 ACS 5-year estimate. As a result, the percent change in annual water and sewer rates, schooling information, population without a computer, and health insurance could not be estimated. Water systems with duplicated boundaries could not be calculated.

**EPIC's data score:** 76%. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 11 different variables that were created after cleaning the crosswalked/interpolated dataset. Combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe, this produced a mean quality score of 76%.

**Recommended uses:** Estimation of how the population characteristics contained within a service area has changed over the past 10 years. Identifying what service areas are serving communities that have rapidly grown or shrunk in people and income.

**Methods:** The census tract and service area boundary crosswalk file was downloaded from the EPA ORD GitHub website; this table uses Microsoft building footprints to weight census data to water system service area boundaries. Data from duplicated systems were removed (specifically: "FL1070685", "FL1190789", "FL6580531", "IA2573701", "MT0001923", "VA5019052"), as they sometimes produced weights greater than one. NHGIS crosswalk files were downloaded to relate 2020 census tracts back to 2010 census geometries.

The EPA ORD crosswalk was merged with the NHGIS crosswalk file, and the total number of Microsoft building footprints was multiplied by the 2010 tract housing weight to estimate the 2010 tract building total (assuming housing weights are correlated with the number of buildings). Unique tract building totals were then grouped and summed by the 2010 census tract GEOID (summing unique values avoids double-counting, since a single tract may overlap with multiple service areas and therefore share the same tract building total). These new building totals were added back to the main crosswalk file.

The number of buildings that overlapped in the ORD crosswalk file was then multiplied by the census tract housing weights from the NHGIS file to estimate how many buildings overlapped with EPA service area boundaries. This final dataset was grouped by water system ID, 2010 census tract, and 2010 census tract Microsoft building totals; the total number of overlapping buildings (after weighting) was summed and divided by the total estimated Microsoft buildings in the 2010 census tract to create a new weight.

Data from the ACS 2011 5-year estimate were collected, and all non-income variables were multiplied by the specific water system and tract weight, grouped by water system ID, and summed to estimate totals at the water system level. Income variables were related to the percentage of the total universe prior to weighted interpolation (using 2020 decennial census household counts as weights), then multiplied back by the total universe after interpolation, adjusted for inflation using procedures similar to the Bureau of Labor Statistics inflation adjuster. Water systems that overlap with multiple states were handled using a mean. If a water system has been operating for less than 10 years (based on the SDWIS water system dataset), values are replaced with "NA". Percent change was calculated as: 100 * ((2021 census variable - 2011 census variable) / 2011 census variable).

## EJScreen {#raw_ejscreen}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_ejscreen -->

**Description:** As described on the tool website, "EJScreen, the Environmental Justice Screening and Mapping Tool, is a free and public online screening and mapping tool that contains environmental and demographic data on different areas of the United States." Originally developed by EPA, now maintained by Public Environmental Data Partners.

**Caveats:** The drinking water score was developed based on an older vintage of the EPA service area boundaries, which were related to the block group level in EJScreen. Since service area boundaries have been updated since this score was created, EPIC is working to recreate this drinking water score at the water system level. Due to inconsistencies between the current SABs and the SABs used in the original EJScreen calculation, the drinking water non-compliance score is not currently available - EPIC hopes to include it in the future based on the latest boundaries provided by the EPA.

**EPIC's data score:** 74%. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 3 different variables created after cleaning the interpolated dataset, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** _TODO: list recommended uses_

**Methods:** Data from EJScreen, as hosted on the Harvard Dataverse website, were downloaded and filtered to remove data from territories (gathering census data for these locations is more difficult, but is on the roadmap for a future version of the tool). This dataset was merged with ACS 2022 block group geometries by GEOID. EJScreen data were estimated to EPA SABs using a mix of interpolation methods: population-focused variables were interpolated using census block populations or households as weights (based on whether the variable is population or household focused), and area-based variables used areal interpolation. For both methods, variables were treated as either spatially intensive (percentiles) or extensive (counts). All spatial datasets were projected to an Albers equal area projection (crs = 5070) prior to interpolating.

## Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool {#raw_cejst}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_cejst -->

**Description:** As described on the source website, "The CEJST uses publicly-available, nationally-consistent datasets to identify disadvantaged communities. The datasets are indicators of burdens that disadvantaged communities face. These burdens are related to climate change, the environment, health, and economic opportunity. The CEJST features a user-friendly, searchable map of all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and the U.S. territories. Communities are considered disadvantaged if they are in census tracts that meet the thresholds for at least one of the tool's categories of burden, or if they are on lands within the boundaries of Federally Recognized Tribes." Maintained by Public Environmental Data Partners.

**Caveats:** Data from CEJST were interpolated (see Methods for details); as a result, some variables for some water systems could not be calculated.

**EPIC's data score:** 74%. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 4 different variables created after cleaning the interpolated dataset, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** Identifying water systems that serve communities identified as disadvantaged by CEJST.

**Methods:** Data from the CEJST, as hosted on the Public Environmental Data Partners website, were downloaded - the shapefile was downloaded to obtain the codebook and census tract geometries, which were combined with the community list data containing the variables of interest. CEJST variables were estimated to EPA SABs using a mix of interpolation methods: population-focused variables were interpolated using census block populations or households as weights, and area-based variables used areal interpolation. For both methods, variables were treated as either spatially intensive (percentiles) or extensive (counts). 2010 census geometries were used to match the vintage of CEJST. All spatial datasets were projected to an Albers equal area projection (crs = 5070) prior to interpolating.

## Social Vulnerability Index {#raw_svi}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_svi -->

**Description:** As described on the source website, "Social vulnerability refers to the demographic and socioeconomic factors (such as poverty, lack of access to transportation, and crowded housing) that adversely affect communities that encounter hazards and other community-level stressors. These stressors can include natural or human-caused disasters (such as tornadoes or chemical spills) or disease outbreaks (such as COVID-19)."

**Caveats:** Data from the SVI were interpolated (see Methods for details); as a result, some variables for some water systems could not be calculated.

**EPIC's data score:** 77%. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 2 different variables created after cleaning the interpolated dataset, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** Identifying water systems that serve communities identified as vulnerable by the SVI.

**Methods:** Data from the SVI were downloaded from the CDC website. For the rpl_themes flag, values of -999 were transformed to NAs; per the documentation, this value means it was unavailable from the original census data, and this avoids the value being interpolated as a true numeric value. Data from the SVI were estimated to EPA SABs using a mix of interpolation methods: population-focused variables were interpolated using census block populations or households as weights, and area-based variables used areal interpolation. For both methods, variables were treated as either spatially intensive (percentiles) or extensive (counts of people, households, etc). The SVI documentation doesn't explicitly state the census vintage, but since many variables are from the ACS 2022 5yr estimate, 2020 census block data were used for weighting. All spatial datasets were projected to an Albers equal area projection (crs = 5070) prior to interpolating.

## Water System Watersheds for Well & Intake Locations {#clean_pwsid_intake_well_huc12}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: clean_pwsid_intake_well_huc12 -->

**Description:** Obtained from the EPA's How's My Waterway? - contains the HUC12 of well and intake locations for water systems.

**Caveats:** N/A.

**EPIC's data score:** 76%. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 8 different variables created after cleaning the dataset. This score checks a summarized dataset that contains data from NPDES, underground storage tanks, facilities with risk management plans, and impaired waterways, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe, producing a mean quality score of 76%.

**Recommended uses:** Identifying which watershed(s) a water system pulls from.

**Methods:** Data were collected via email, and the dataset was filtered to only contain records from EPA's community water system service area boundary dataset.

## Climate Vulnerability Index {#raw_cvi}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_cvi -->

**Description:** Maintained by the Environmental Defense Fund. As described on the source website, "The U.S. Climate Vulnerability Index helps you see which communities face the greatest challenges from the impacts of a changing climate. This tool shows what is driving the challenges, so policymakers and communities themselves can take action to build climate resilience where it is needed most."

**Caveats:** Data from the CVI were interpolated (see Methods for details); as a result, some variables for some water systems could not be calculated.

**EPIC's data score:** 77%. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 5 different variables created after cleaning the interpolated dataset, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** Identifying water systems that serve communities vulnerable to climate change.

**Methods:** Data from the CVI were downloaded using the Master CVI dataset from the EDF website (containing overall climate vulnerability and percentile scores) and related to 2010 census geographies. Data were estimated to EPA SABs using a mix of interpolation methods: population-focused variables were interpolated using census block populations or households as weights, and area-based variables used areal interpolation. For both methods, variables were treated as either spatially intensive (percentiles) or extensive (counts). 2010 census geometries were used to match the vintage of the CVI. All spatial datasets were projected to an Albers equal area projection (crs = 5070) prior to interpolating.

## National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Permits {#raw_npdes_permits}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_npdes_permits -->

**Description:** Outfalls data from the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) from EPA's ECHO database. "The NPDES permit program addresses water pollution by regulating point sources that discharge pollutants to waters of the United States. Created in 1972 by the Clean Water Act, the NPDES permit program is authorized to state governments by EPA to perform many permitting, administrative, and enforcement aspects of the program."

**Caveats:** If a water system is pulling from a watershed that contains a lot of permitted outfalls, that does not necessarily mean the drinking water quality is at risk or of poor quality - water systems employ a variety of treatment techniques to filter contaminants from the source water. This variable is aimed at communicating potential hazards, rather than an actual risk to drinking water. Since permitted features were sorted into HUC12s (and a single permit number may apply to multiple features), a single external_permit_nmbr may match to multiple HUC12s - so a permit in violation could show up in multiple HUCs, even if that specific feature within the HUC12 is not in violation.

**EPIC's data score:** 76%. This score checks a summarized dataset that contains data from NPDES, underground storage tanks, facilities with risk management plans, and impaired waterways. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 8 different variables, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** Identifying what water systems are pulling from a watershed that contains a certain amount of permitted discharge outfalls.

**Methods:** NPDES permits were downloaded using the ECHO outfalls layer. Data were filtered to contain permits with "Effective", "Admin Continued", or "Pending" status (permit_status_dec), and permits with locations outside of the U.S. were removed (the U.S. boundary was buffered to 50 miles offshore, and `st_within` was used to capture permits within 50 miles of the shoreline - not the technical definition of WOTUS, but sufficient since this is related to HUC12s, which are on land). Point data were then sorted into HUC12s (looping through each state, retrieving HUC12s, and matching CRS before running an `st_intersection` with spherical geometry turned off), which further removed offshore permits or permits with geometry errors.

Data were simplified to permit-level data (feature codes and lat/longs removed, since they contained duplicated permit data), grouped by HUC12, and the total number of unique external permit numbers (external_permit_nmbr) was counted, along with those with violations (cwa_current_status is "violation identified" or "significant/category I noncompliance"), those with significant violations (cwa_current_status is "significant/category I noncompliance"), and those with effluent violations (cwp_current_snc_status is "Effluent - Monthly Average Limit" or "Effluent - Non-monthly Average Limit"). Violation data reflect the most current data available, including data reported after the last quarterly noncompliance report was issued.

Since permitted features were sorted into HUC12s (and a single permit number may apply to multiple features), a single external_permit_nmbr may match to multiple HUC12s, so a permit in violation could show up in multiple HUCs even if that specific feature is not in violation - fixing this would require sorting through discharge monitoring reports by permitted feature, which is computationally intensive (~400,000 permits) and could be considered in a future version. If a permitted feature exists at the nexus of multiple HUC12s, the data for that permit is duplicated across those overlapping HUC12s. All spatial datasets were projected to an Albers equal area projection (crs = 5070) prior to running intersections.

## 303(d) Impaired Waterways {#raw_imp_waters}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_imp_waters -->

**Description:** Data from assessed streams - state water quality assessment decisions reported to EPA under the Integrated Report (IR), and Clean Water Act Sections 303(d) and 305(b). This service provides summary information for each Assessment Unit. For more detailed data, see the Assessment Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL) Tracking and Implementation System (ATTAINS) web services, documented at the public ATTAINS website.

**Caveats:** This information is reported by states, and the amount of assessed waters and streams varies across states. If a water system is pulling from a watershed that contains many impaired waterways, that does not necessarily mean the drinking water quality is at risk or of poor quality - water systems employ a variety of treatment techniques to filter contaminants from the source water. This variable is aimed at communicating potential hazards, rather than an actual risk to drinking water.

**EPIC's data score:** 76%. This score checks a summarized dataset that contains data from NPDES, underground storage tanks, facilities with risk management plans, and impaired waterways. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 8 different variables, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** Identifying what water systems are pulling from a watershed that contains a certain amount of impaired waterways.

**Methods:** Data were downloaded from ArcGIS REST services, grouped by HUC12, and summarized to identify the number of assessed streams, how many of those are impaired or threatened, and how many are on a 303(d) list (impaired stream without a TMDL). These sums are based on the presence of "Y" in the assessed, impaired, threatened, and on303dlist fields. The not_assessed column was based on the presence of "N" in the isassessed column. All of these data are state-reported from the ATTAINS web services, and there is significant variation between states.

Based on the ATTAINS metadata: **isassessed** - if the state has monitored a water and made an Assessment decision about the Assessment Unit, it is considered Assessed; if the state has defined the Assessment Unit but has not yet monitored and assessed it, it is Not Assessed. **impaired** - if any part of the Assessment Unit fails to meet its water quality standards, it is calculated as impaired. **threatened** - one or more Uses is Fully Supporting but experiencing a declining trend and likely to become impaired in the next reporting cycle; threatened waters are part of the CWA Section 303(d) list unless a TMDL has been created for them (a null value is the same as isThreatened = 'N'). **303(d) list** - if the Assessment Unit is impaired by a pollutant and still needs to be addressed by a TMDL or other pollution control measure, it falls on the CWA Section 303(d) List (also known as EPA IR Category 5); this does not include all impaired waters (e.g. Assessment Units already covered by a TMDL fall into EPA IR Category 4a and are not on the 303(d) list).

All spatial datasets were projected to an Albers equal area projection (crs = 5070) prior to running intersections.

## Underground Storage Tanks {#raw_open_usts}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_open_usts -->

**Description:** Point data containing the locations of facilities with active underground storage tanks, from the UST Finder - "a flexible web application containing a comprehensive, national map of underground storage tank (UST) and UST release data. UST Finder provides the attributes and locations of active and closed USTs, UST facilities, and UST releases in states, tribal lands, and U.S. territories." Developed by EPA in partnership with the Association of State and Territorial Solid Waste Management Officials (ASTSWMO). This information was collected from September 2018 through December 2019 and represents a snapshot of UST facilities at the time of data collection. Information on UST releases is not summarized, as these events are typically resolved in 1-2 years and the dataset was deemed too old to include in the application.

**Caveats:** If a water system is pulling from a watershed that contains a lot of open underground storage tanks, that does not necessarily mean the drinking water quality is at risk or of poor quality - water systems employ a variety of treatment techniques to filter contaminants from the source water. This variable is aimed at communicating potential hazards, rather than an actual risk to drinking water. This dataset is static, and only contains a snapshot of information collected from September 2018 - December 2019. Because the exact location of underground storage tanks is not provided, it is assumed that facilities with underground storage tanks are close in proximity to the storage tanks they manage.

**EPIC's data score:** 76%. This score checks a summarized dataset that contains data from NPDES, underground storage tanks, facilities with risk management plans, and impaired waterways. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 8 different variables, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** Identifying what water systems are pulling from a watershed that contains a certain amount of open underground storage tanks.

**Methods:** Point data were downloaded using ArcGIS REST services and filtered to only contain records whose facility status is active. Point data were sorted into HUC12s (points without geometry or those outside of the U.S. were removed; HUC12s were retrieved per-state and the CRS matched to the UST data before running an `st_intersection` with spherical geometry turned off), grouped by HUC12, and the total number of open underground storage tanks was summed using the open_usts field and temporarily out-of-service USTs (considered "open" by EPA standards). All spatial datasets were projected to an Albers equal area projection (crs = 5070) prior to running intersections.

## Facilities with Risk Management Plans {#raw_rmp_sites}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_rmp_sites -->

**Description:** Facilities with active risk management plans - EPA's Facility Registry Service (FRS) subset of facilities that link to the Risk Management Plan (RMP) database. "The Risk Management Plan (RMP) database stores the risk management plans reported by companies that handle, manufacture, use, or store certain flammable or toxic substances, as required under section 112(r) of the Clean Air Act (CAA)."

**Caveats:** If a water system is pulling from a watershed that contains a lot of facilities with risk management plans, that does not necessarily mean the drinking water quality is at risk or of poor quality - water systems employ a variety of treatment techniques to filter contaminants from the source water. This variable is aimed at communicating potential hazards, rather than an actual risk to drinking water.

**EPIC's data score:** 76%. This score checks a summarized dataset that contains data from NPDES, underground storage tanks, facilities with risk management plans, and impaired waterways. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 8 different variables, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** Identifying what water systems are pulling from a watershed that contains a certain amount of facilities with risk management plans.

**Methods:** Point data were downloaded using ArcGIS REST services and filtered to only contain records whose facility status is "active". Point data were sorted into HUC12s (HUC12s were retrieved per-state and the CRS matched to the RMP sites before running an `st_intersection` with spherical geometry turned off), grouped by HUC12, and the total number of facilities with Risk Management Plans was summed using the number of unique registry IDs within each HUC12. All spatial datasets were projected to an Albers equal area projection (crs = 5070) prior to running intersections.

# Boil Water Notice Datasets

## Oregon Drinking Water Advisories {#raw_or_bwn}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_or_bwn -->

**Description:** Publicly available drinking water advisories for water systems located in Oregon, provided by the Oregon Public Health Authority - Drinking Water Data Online.

**Caveats:** Continuous data collection started October 2nd, 2025, and updates are completed quarterly - refer to the source link for the most current information. Some drinking water advisories may reflect planned maintenance rather than a contaminant or infrastructure event; EPIC hopes to distinguish these in the future if possible with the data available. To account for differences in the scale of reporting between states, it is assumed a water system reports a maximum of one advisory on a given day. If a state edits the date an advisory was reported or lifted after it has been filled out, this is captured as a new advisory - it is difficult to discern edited advisories from completely new ones.

**EPIC's data score:** 76%. This score checks a summarized dataset containing data for all states with boil water notice and advisory data. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 10 different variables, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** Screening for water systems that have had disruptions in service.

**Methods:** Oregon boil water notice data were scraped from the state webpage in R. Water system IDs were fixed by appending "OR41" to the PWS column, and boil water notices that appeared prior to 2017 were removed, since water advisory tracking began in May 2017 and most advisories from before that time are not displayed. Data are updated by pulling the latest webpage data in R and checking it against data from the last pull in S3; records are updated (e.g. if they have closed since the last pull) and new records are added. Data were filtered to only records for CWS.

## West Virginia Drinking Water Advisories {#raw_wv_bwn}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_wv_bwn -->

**Description:** Publicly available drinking water advisories for water systems located in West Virginia, provided by the WV Department of Health and Human Resources.

**Caveats:** A water system in this dataset may report multiple, potentially separate advisories on the same day - for example, a system may report multiple advisories for each area affected by the same main break, so the number of advisories for this state may appear very large compared to other states. To account for differences in the scale of reporting between states, it is assumed a water system reports a maximum of one advisory on a given day. If a state edits the date an advisory was reported or lifted after it has been filled out, this is captured as a new advisory. Continuous data collection started October 2nd, 2025, and updates are completed quarterly - refer to the source link for the most current information. Some drinking water advisories may reflect planned maintenance rather than a contaminant or infrastructure event.

**EPIC's data score:** 76%. This score checks a summarized dataset containing data for all states with boil water notice and advisory data. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 10 different variables, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** Screening for water systems that have had disruptions in service.

**Methods:** The state webpage was inspected and the API endpoint containing these data was located. Data were read into R and filtered to only contain data for community water systems. Data are updated by pulling the latest API data in R and checking it against data from the last pull in S3; records are updated (e.g. if they have closed since the last pull) and new records are added. Because the method creates a unique ID using the date the advisory was issued to detect dataset updates, records that have been edited may appear as a separate advisory.

## Texas Drinking Water Advisories {#raw_tx_bwn}

<!-- CONFIG METADATA: raw_tx_bwn -->

**Description:** FOIA'd drinking water advisories for water systems located in Texas, provided by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ).

**Caveats:** This dataset only contains records from 2018-2024. The last update occurred on April 17th, 2024 - this is not a comprehensive record, and EPIC is working to automatically update this dataset in the future. Refer to the source link (the state SDWIS website) for the most current information. Some drinking water advisories may reflect planned maintenance rather than a contaminant or infrastructure event. To account for differences in the scale of reporting between states, it is assumed a water system reports a maximum of one advisory on a given day. If a state edits the date an advisory was reported or lifted after it has been filled out, this is captured as a new advisory.

**EPIC's data score:** 76%. This score checks a summarized dataset containing data for all states with boil water notice and advisory data. To create this score, EPIC checked for data completeness (how many "NA"s are there?) and how many duplicated records exist (if applicable) across 10 different variables, combined with an estimate for how well these variables reflect the larger data universe.

**Recommended uses:** Screening for water systems that have had disruptions in service.

**Methods:** Data were FOIA'd from TCEQ on April 17th, 2024. Issued and rescinded dates were converted to proper date formats; an issued date in 2027 was removed and assumed to be an error. These dates were converted to standardized "date_issued" and "date_lifted" fields (using the dates likely entered by the utility, rather than the reported_date/achieved_date fields, which have similar/identical definitions). Four events are missing date_issued, and 10 events have a value >= 1 in the "reissued count" field; since these are folded into the same date_issued, they are treated as a single boil water notice event for the utility rather than duplicated. Data were then filtered for water systems with service area boundaries from the EPA.
